catalog_quote: 5. All syllables are open in Muna. There are no consonant clusters. The only syllable patterns are therefore V and CV. The prenasalized consonants are analyzed as phonemic units; they occur both initially and medially. [...] 6. Two consecutive identical vowels belong to different syllables. Phonetically such a combination is a long vowel: la.a [la:] 'river' ne.e [ne:] 'nose' 7. Stress is almost invariably penultimate in Muna. This is also true for the other dialects and languages to be discussed. Stress is therefore not marked. [...] [p. 44:] During my stay on Muna and Buton I collected wordlists in the following non-Muna speech communities: [...] 3. Liabuku (LIA), about 10 km north of Baubau. This is the first non-Wolio speaking village on the road from Baubau towards Kapontori.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (32-page scan, no text layer; per-page tesseract scanned in scanned/). I rendered PDF page 8 (printed p. 27) to PNG and read it visually: section 2 'Standard Muna phonology', point 7 reads exactly 'Stress is almost invariably penultimate in Muna. This is also true for the other dialects and languages to be discussed. Stress is therefore not marked.' -- verbatim as reported. Points 5-6 on the same page (all syllables open, V/CV only; identical vowel sequences disyllabic) also match the first reader's domain note. The second half of the quote (p. 44 = PDF p. 25, sec. 6 'Pancanic isolects') is also verbatim modulo the marked ellipses: 'During my stay on Muna and Buton I collected…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable ('almost invariably'), stated for Standard Muna and explicitly extended by the author to all the other Muna dialects and Munic/Pancanic languages treated in the paper, which include Liabuku (author's own wordlist collected in Liabuku village). Stress is therefore left unmarked in all cited forms.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'almost invariably' (no Liabuku-specific exceptions given). For Muna proper, van den Berg 2003:94 (PL-550, on file) notes siua 'nine' keeps antepenultimate stress after glide syllabification; that remark concerns Muna, not Liabuku.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement based on wordlist (citation-form) data; blanket statement covering all isolects in the paper rather than a dedicated Liabuku phonology. Syllables are all open (V, CV) and identical vowel sequences are disyllabic in Muna (same page), so 'penultimate syllable' = penultimate vowel.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is a blanket one: van den Berg (1991:27) describes Standard Muna and says penultimate stress 'is also true for the other dialects and languages to be discussed', which include Liabuku (LIA, his own wordlist from Liabuku village ~10 km N of Baubau; grouped with Pancana, Kioko, Kambowa as 'Pancanic', pp. 44-45) = Glottolog liab1237. There is no dedicated Liabuku phonology anywhere. Classification differs across sources: Glottolog/van den Berg put Liabuku in Munic (Western Munic/Pancanic); Ethnologue/Wikipedia call it a divergent Muna dialect; Indonesia's Badan Bahasa Peta Bahasa (Labbineka 'Bahasa Wolio') instead counts 'dialek Liabuku' (Kel. Liabuku, Kec. Bungi, Kota Baubau) as a Wolio dialect by dialectometry (51-78% difference) -- same village, different lumping. van den Berg 2001 (pers. comm. on sulang.org) also notes Liabuku and the 'Todanga' dialect are reportedly mutually intelligible.
